However, scaling this approach remains challenging because larger images require increasingly many binary variables and interactions in the underlying quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. Even with iterative region-of-interest (ROI) refinement, a 60 by 60 ROI with three X-ray mass attenuation coefficients requires 10,800 binary variables under our encoding. As an initial step toward larger quantum CT images, we investigate simulated annealing (SA) followed by spin-error mitigation for optimisation (SEMO), without altering the CT-QUBO objective. We evaluate three 54-view ROI reconstruction instances and nine-view reconstruction with detector-row corruption, comparing SA and SEMO with selected hybrid quantum-classical solver results. For the ROI cases, SEMO reduced the numbers of incorrectly reconstructed pixels in low-budget SA outputs from 13 to 1, 38 to 0, and 54 to 15. With 20 percent detector-row corruption, three of four selected SA and SEMO pairs achieved exact reconstruction. Applying SEMO to one hybrid-solver output reduced its ROI error from 78 to 1 pixel. Improvements were instance-dependent: in one corrupted-sinogram case, QUBO energy decreased while image-domain error increased slightly; in one ROI case, the refined image retained 15 incorrect pixels despite having lower QUBO energy than ground truth. At the evaluated problem sizes, SA and SEMO attained reconstruction accuracy comparable to or better than selected unmitigated hybrid-solver results, providing an initial solution-quality benchmark for future larger-scale, parallelized quantum CT image reconstruction.

pending.title: Geometric aspects of fault tolerance
pending.abstract: We highlight three geometric aspects of fault tolerance. First, we construct an operator-algebraic formulation of the fiber bundle framework for fault tolerance, and show that a generalization of the Knill-Laflamme conditions implies a flat connection for this framework. Next, we develop this framework for Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. We show that, for each polarization type, their moduli space embeds smoothly into a Grassmannian of finite-dimensional subspaces of a regularized distribution space. Finally, we explain how GKP codes associated with Jacobians give rise to magic states that can be obtained by code space projections of Gaussian states and identify a $\rm CCZ$-type magic state arising this way.

pending.title: Fast and accurate rare-event simulation by Markov chain Monte Carlo for general quantum codes
pending.abstract: The splitting method estimates logical error rates of quantum error-correcting codes deep in the rare-event regime, where direct Monte Carlo sampling is prohibitively expensive. It relies on a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler of faulty configurations, usually driven by one-bit-flip proposals. However, one-bit flips have been reported to be trapped on some codes, which biases the estimate. To address this issue, we propose a new kernel that combines locally balanced one-bit-flip proposals with a cluster-exchange move. We benchmark both kernels and direct Monte Carlo on twelve codes under code-capacity bit-flip noise in two ways, by comparing the mean fault weight with an MCMC-independent reference and by measuring the computation time to reach a fixed accuracy. In the first, our kernel agrees with the reference on every code, including those where one-bit flips are trapped. In the second, it is faster than one-bit flips wherever they are trapped, by orders of magnitude on some codes. Furthermore, at the lowest error rate, it is faster than direct Monte Carlo on every code, by more than four orders of magnitude on some.

pending.title: Multipartite dynamics beyond bipartite entanglement equilibration
pending.abstract: Entanglement equilibration need not mark the end of quantum-information dynamics in quantum thermalization. We show that the complete Schmidt spectra of a fixed tripartition can become stationary while its multipartite correlation structure, distinguished by local-unitary invariants, continues to evolve. This separation occurs exactly within a finite window in self-dual kicked-Ising dynamics and asymptotically in Haar-random circuits. We further demonstrate an independently tunable timescale for multipartite dynamics using quantum-error-correcting codes. When coupled to a locally scrambling bath, ordinary entanglement approaches equilibrium through rapid local scrambling, while weak logical--bath coupling drives a slower reorganization of multipartite correlations. These results reveal a deeper distinction than the ordering of equilibration times: bipartite entanglement and multipartite correlation structure can probe distinct physical channels of quantum-information dynamics, rather than merely different stages of the same relaxation process.

pending.title: Sublinear thermal state and ground state preparation for free fermions via system-bath interaction
pending.abstract: Dissipative algorithms for preparing thermal and ground states typically require a total Hamiltonian simulation time that grows at least linearly with system size $N$, even when their mixing time grows only polylogarithmically. We achieve sublinear simulation time for free fermions by engineering local interactions with a bath whose size grows in proportion to the system size. Starting from arbitrary initial states, our thermal state preparation algorithm achieves trace-norm error $ε$ in total simulation time $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{N}/ε)$ at fixed inverse temperature and bounded single-particle bandwidth, while ground state preparation of gapped systems requires only $\mathrm{polylog}(N/ε)$ time. We further establish lower bounds for thermal state preparation within the bath protocols considered, identifying two obstacles to faster preparation, namely fourth-order deviations from the target thermal state and fluctuations induced by a random frequency shared by all bath qubits. Our results demonstrate that the linear simulation time barrier in dissipative state preparation can be overcome and clarify the bath and filter-design constraints that govern further complexity improvements.

pending.title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
pending.abstract: Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

pending.title: Sharp Bounds for Graph-Codes Avoiding Complete Bipartite Differences
pending.abstract: Let $d_{K_{s,t}}(n)$ be the largest fraction of all graphs on $[n]$ in a family containing no two distinct members whose symmetric difference is a copy of $K_{s,t}$. We determine this maximum density for every fixed pair of positive integers $s,t$. If both part sizes are odd, it is known that the density is exactly $1/2$. Otherwise, let $2h$ be the largest even part size. We prove $$ d_{K_{s,t}}(n)=Θ_{s,t}(n^{-h}). $$ For $h>1$, this improves the general $O_{s,t}(1/n)$ upper bound obtained from Alon's two-copy gluing theorem~\cite{Alon2024}. The sharp bounds for even stars were already proved by Alon and are recovered as special cases. The upper bound uses the Frankl--Füredi forbidden-intersection theorem. For the lower bound, we construct binary linear codes using BCH codes. When exactly one part size is even, we assign to each edge the sum of the binary vectors assigned to its endpoints. When both part sizes are even, we identify these vectors with elements of a finite field and assign to each edge the product of its endpoint elements. In both cases, every copy of $K_{s,t}$ has a nonzero syndrome.

pending.title: New families of additive non-RS MDS codes and ACD codes from twisted Reed-Solomon codes
pending.abstract: Additive codes generalize linear codes and play an important role in the construc?tion of quantum codes. As generalizations of linear MDS codes, additive MDS codes have received much research attention. As an important subclass of additive codes, ACD codes are widely used for quantum error correction. In this paper, we study single-twist additive generalized twisted Reed-Solomon (GTRS) codes over finite fields. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for these codes to be MDS for arbitrary hook and twist parameters. Then we employ Schur squares to prove that such additive MDS codes are not monomially equivalent to additive Reed-Solomon codes. We also identify a class of additive GTRS codes whose duals remain additive GTRS codes, and show that, for all sufficiently large prime powers q whose characteristic avoids a finite set, such GTRS codes yield ACD codes.

pending.title: Self-Correcting 3D Surface Code with Growing Local Dimension
pending.abstract: We construct self-correcting 3D surface codes over $\mathbb Z_q$ with local dimension $q$ growing with system size. The model preserves the local geometry and stabilizer support of the ordinary 3D surface code and remains translation invariant in the bulk, while modifying only the stabilizer Pauli powers. We use the Lee metric to characterize error weight and consider local Metropolis dynamics with single-qudit $X^{\pm1}$ and $Z^{\pm1}$ updates, each changing the energy by at most a constant independent of $q$ and system size $N$. We prove that, below the critical temperature, when the local dimension scales as $q=Θ(N)$, the memory times in both error sectors grow at least as $\exp\left[Ω(N^{1/3})\right]$. Our numerical results further support these analytical results. Together, these results establish growing local Hilbert-space dimension as a new resource for designing self-correcting quantum memories while retaining simple local geometry and local thermal dynamics.

pending.title: Higher Order OTOCs in Chaotic Quantum Maps: Ruelle-Pollicott Resonances and Asymptotic Freeness
pending.abstract: Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) measure the scrambling of information and are a powerful diagnostic of chaos. In chaotic quantum systems with a classical analog, their relaxation towards equilibrium is dictated by the classical Ruelle--Pollicott resonances. We investigate higher-order OTOCs in quantum maps, prototypical one-body systems with a classical limit showing all the essential features of chaotic dynamics. We demonstrate numerically that in the intermediate-time regime they decay exponentially at a rate that depends only on the parity of the order: odd-order OTOCs decay at the same rate as classical correlations, given by the leading Ruelle--Pollicott resonance, and even-order ones at twice that rate. Both are far slower than the naive expectation, under which the rate would grow in proportion to the order. We then mimic the effect of an environment by defining a coarse-grained superoperator whose effect is to introduce decoherence into the system, and find that the expected proportionality between rate and order is thereby restored. Finally, we show that at long times each higher-order OTOC becomes dominated by a single free cumulant, whose saturation value falls off inversely with the dimension of the Hilbert space, signalling the emergence of asymptotic freeness and highlighting the relevance of free probability theory as a framework for the study of quantum chaos.

pending.title: QQLink: A Declarative Framework for Multi-QPU Quantum Workflow Orchestration
pending.abstract: Distributed quantum protocols require measurement outcomes produced at one node to control operations at another. We present QQLink, a programming and orchestration layer that expresses these dependencies in a single program, using workflow nodes, deferred measurement references, and declared entanglement, and derives the cross-node coordination automatically. Its planner constructs a provably acyclic dependency graph in time linear in the total size of the instructions' qubit footprints. The same programs execute through simulator backends or are lowered to dynamic circuits on partitioned quantum hardware. We evaluate seven protocol workflows. Exhaustive feedforward-branch tests on the simulator runtime path, over tomographically complete input sets, yield output-state infidelities of at most $5\times10^{-12}$ and no incorrect classical outputs, and replaying every plan in random topological orders leaves each final state unchanged. Separate executor processes run the plans with delayed messages, with the joint quantum state held by a centralized simulation service. Every run with the full plan is correct, and removing required cross-node dependencies causes protocol failures. The lowered circuits match hand-written implementations of the same construction in two-qubit gate and conditional-block counts. Runs on two IBM Heron processors, each partitioned into virtual QPUs, demonstrate same-chip execution in two sessions a week apart. The runs also show large variation between sessions and losses beyond what calibration-derived noise models predict. Coherence-sensitive checks do not establish coherent Toffoli operation or preservation of the intended repetition-code superposition. These results support QQLink's workflow semantics on the tested execution paths and identify limits of the current hardware realization; execution across physically networked QPUs remains future work.

pending.title: Ancilla-free optimal quantum adder
pending.abstract: We construct an exact $n$-bit quantum adder with $O(n)$ gates and $O(\log n)$ depth that requires no ancillary qubits. The circuit uses only $X$, CNOT, and Toffoli gates under all-to-all connectivity and is classically reversible. Our construction accelerates the controlled ladder underlying addition. Grouping the data into blocks and use existing control qubits as conditional workspace gives a recursive construction with $O(n\log\log n)$ gates and $O(\log n)$ depth. We then coordinate inter-block propagation via two short-path forest operations to cut the per-block workspace requirement, yielding a nonrecursive implementation with $O(n)$ gates. Both the gate count and circuit depth are asymptotically optimal.

pending.title: Maximum-Likelihood Decoding of Gabidulin Codes Is NP-Hard Even in Dimension One
pending.abstract: Fix a prime power q. We prove that deciding whether a received word y in Fnqm lies at rank distance at most n-2 from the one-dimensional Gabidulin code {{λ.g : λ in Fqm } is NP-complete. Thus maximum-likelihood decoding of Gabidulin codes is NP-hard even for k = 1, an analogue of the Guruswami-Vardy theorem for Reed-Solomon codes. In the Hamming metric, by contrast, hardness at this radius requires the dimension to grow with the length, as in the Guruswami-Vardy theorem. The reduction is deterministic; consequently Rank Syndrome Decoding (RSD) and Rank Minimum Distance (RMD) for Fqm -linear codes are NP-complete under deterministic polynomial reductions, whereas the previously known reduction was randomized. The proof goes through a pivot problem that we introduce, Twisted Square Membership (TSM): given Fq-subspaces U, W in FqN , decide whether some non-zero a in U satisfies a^(q+1) in W . Quadratic systems in d unknowns are encoded into TSM, then TSM into Gabidulin decoding. The last step views the received word as an Fq-linear map and decoding at radius n - 2 as the search for an Fq-plane on which it acts as a scalar. With support U + τ W in a cubic extension and map a + τ b to a^(q^2) + τ bq^q , two Frobenius twists force solution planes to encode the relation a^(q+1) in W . All constructions are explicit and polynomial, with N = O(qd^2 ), n less than N + d, and m = 3N .

pending.title: Resource-Optimal Screening for Two-Tier Quantum System Characterization
pending.abstract: Quantum processing units (QPUs) require frequent benchmarking to track hardware drift, yet standard protocols such as randomized benchmarking are resource-intensive and compete with application workloads for scarce QPU time. We present a resource-optimal screening strategy that combines a two-tier, risk-based testing architecture with optimal experiment design: a lightweight screening probe runs regularly and triggers expensive full characterization only when statistically significant change is detected, while the probe itself is designed to maximize detection sensitivity under explicit resource constraints. For an exponential fidelity model, we derive closed-form optimal circuit sizes and introduce an effective gate count that renders the analysis hardware-independent. We instantiate the strategy for two applications. For gate-quality verification, we show that optimally designed screening probes outperform randomized benchmarking with optimal experimental design (OED) by more than 4$\times$ in detection rate at equal resource cost. For compiler benchmarking, we formalize compiler comparison as a paired hypothesis test and derive the optimal circuit size for distinguishing compilation strategies. Despite their different observables and test statistics, both applications yield structurally the same closed-form expression for the optimal probe circuit size as a function of gate fidelity, illustrating the generality of the framework. Numerical and hardware experiments on QPUs (Rigetti Ankaa-3, IQM Garnet, IQM Emerald) confirm the theoretical predictions, with observed optimal circuit sizes matching the derived values across all devices.

pending.title: Initial-State Preparation for Strongly Correlated Molecules from Matrix Product States: Benchmarking and Environment-Aware Divide-and-Conquer Compilation
pending.abstract: Compiling classically optimized matrix product states (MPSs) into quantum circuits is a promising route to initial-state preparation for strongly correlated molecules, but the accuracy, gate cost, and classical scalability of existing MPS compilation methods have not been systematically assessed. Here, we benchmark representative analytical, variational, and hybrid MPS compilation methods for strongly correlated systems including hydrogen chains and iron-sulfur clusters. We compare state infidelity, CNOT gate count, classical runtime, and parallel scalability across different system sizes and bond dimensions. We also introduce a divide-and-conquer environment-aware compilation algorithm (DCE), which optimizes each local isometry approximation according to its contribution to the prepared-state fidelity. The results reveal complementary operating regimes: direct variational compilation methods are gate-efficient for some smaller molecular systems with $O(10)$ qubits and $O(10)$ bond dimensions or moderate accuracy targets with infidelity of order $10^{-1}$, whereas divide-and-conquer methods scale more favorably for larger systems and relatively higher bond dimensions of $O(10\text{-}10^2)$, particularly when target infidelities below $10^{-1}$ are required. Within the latter family, environment-aware optimization improves accuracy over unitary-distance-based compilation while retaining task-level parallelism. For the FeMo-cofactor (FeMoco), we find the DCE algorithm together with the MPS obtained in the entanglement-minimized orbitals (EMOs) provides a resource-efficient route to initial-state preparation. Our results provide practical guidance for selecting and developing MPS compilation methods for strongly correlated molecular simulations.

pending.title: Task-Directed Spectral Design for Local Quantum Tomography
pending.abstract: Many tomography tasks require only a low-dimensional function of the state. We study local pure-state tomography under projective-fidelity access when a parametric model, a credible center, and a differentiable downstream task are known before acquisition. The pullback Fubini--Study metric and the task metric define coordinate-invariant generalized eigendirections, which we realize as a fixed library of geodesic fidelity probes. We prove two optimality results: the probe aligned with a task coordinate is its unique variance-minimizing location up to orientation, and, when prior and measurement information are diagonal in this basis, a diminishing-return greedy rule exactly minimizes the integer-budget local task-variance surrogate over the spectral library. Under common per-shot information and the stated large-budget condition, the absolute and relative gaps to arbitrary probe directions are respectively \(O(B^{-3})\) and \(O(B^{-2})\). A closed-form local estimator is followed by a task-metric localization projection that cannot increase quadratic task loss when localization holds. In six-qubit numerical experiments, the Schmidt-spectrum design activates only one or two settings and has lower mean task error than the post hoc best adaptive results across all tested dimensions and copy budgets. For full-state tomography, it likewise has lower mean infidelity throughout the tested local regime. The fixed batch uses no feedback loops and far fewer settings; under the illustrative latency model, its acquisition cost is roughly three to four orders of magnitude lower than that of the adaptive methods.

pending.title: Competing Fault Histories in Lattice-Surgery Decoding
pending.abstract: Different physical faults can produce the same detector record while carrying opposite logical labels. We investigate the consequence of this ambiguity for a lattice surgery parity measurement. In a distance-three merge--split circuit, single-gate faults compete with reset/readout pairs on three complete syndromes. Full-syndrome probabilities give a simultaneous 95\% lower confidence bound of $16.64$ parts per million on the cost of retaining the selected single-fault decisions at one noise point. Changing those decisions is harmful at low noise and beneficial at higher noise. To test the physical explanation, we attenuate eight implicated channels and compare the change in override effect with a matched non-target suppression. The two interventions change the decoder effect differently, resolving a contribution associated with those locations. Likelihood predictions fixed before sampling then select useful decisions under mixed Pauli noise and after extending preparation and recovery. The latter test gives a reduction of $13.20$ parts per million, with simultaneous 95\% bounds $[5.55,20.84]$. The mechanism is limited in scope: the revised decisions give up certain single-fault corrections, and under the same witness-selection rule no candidate is identified in the fully expanded distance-five circuit. These results connect a finite-noise decoding trade-off to specific physical channels and test how far that explanation can be used to predict logical-parity performance.

pending.title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA
pending.abstract: Quantum computing offers promising approaches to combinatorial optimization problems whose search spaces grow exponentially with problem size. The Closest String problem belongs to this category, which seeks a string that minimizes the maximum Hamming distance to any string in a given collection of reference strings. In this work, we present an end-to-end quantum implementation of the Closest String problem using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA), evaluating its resource requirements and solution amplification capabilities. Our automated workflow converts arbitrary problem instances into quantum circuits expressed in one- or two-qubit gates that encode candidate solutions, evaluate the objective function, and apply NV-QWOA optimisation to increase the measurement probabilities of high-quality solutions. Analytical resource estimates yield a qubit complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nm\log k)$ and a circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(pm\log^2 n + pn\log n)$, where $n$ is the string length, $m$ is the number of reference strings, $k$ is the alphabet size, and $p$ is the number of NV-QWOA iterations. We introduce a revised prescription for the phase-separation parameter, $γ$, that depends on problem size but requires no instance-specific optimization. This prescription mitigates excessive phase wrapping modulo $2π$, which can weaken the relationship between objective values and the phases guiding the optimization dynamics. Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal candidates. This work provides an explicit gate-level implementation, an improved phase-scaling method, and a foundation for hardware experiments and benchmarking against classical algorithms.

pending.title: Junction Hook Errors in the Color Code
pending.abstract: Color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules have been proposed to mitigate hook errors in the triangular color code. Recent work by Kishony and Fowler (arXiv:2603.28852) identifies distance-reducing hook errors by the type of anyon for which they provide a shortcut and chooses the CNOT ordering for stabilizers of each color to avoid these errors. We identify an additional class of distance-reducing hooks, which we call junction hook errors, that is not captured by this classification. The two data qubits of a junction hook error terminate anyon strings of two different colors at the point where the three colored strings of a logical operator meet, which we call the junction. As such, the hook error does not correspond to a single type of anyon, yet it still reduces the distance. For distances $d=7,9,11$, we verify that every non-corner plaquette admits a scheduled hook error that, together with $d-2$ single data qubit faults, produces an undetectable logical error using $d-1$ faults. Each of these is a junction hook error. Because of this, every stabilizer, including those in the bulk, still requires additional protection from hook errors (such as flag qubits) to restore the full circuit-level distance with this schedule. A minimum weight logical operator has at most one junction, however, so junction hook errors cannot accumulate on one minimum weight logical operator in the way that single-color malign hook errors can. This helps explain why the schedule still improves the circuit-level distance to $d-\lfloor (d+3)/6\rfloor$, rather than the $d/2$ distance associated with spatially uniform color code scheduling.

pending.title: Twirled and swirled worlds: a compositional approach
pending.abstract: Twirled and swirled worlds describe generalised probabilistic theories (GPTs) restricted by symmetry-imposed superselection rules. We extend these constructions to a fully compositional setting for finite-dimensional GPTs and compact groups, treating states, effects, and multipartite transformations uniformly as processes. We distinguish system actions from process-space actions. We define actions on a theory as a whole by requiring the corresponding process-space actions to respect sequential and parallel composition. Averaging physical theory actions defines twirling, while averaging nonphysical theory actions defines swirling. We show that invariant subtheories might not satisfy process tomography, and establish conditions under which they do, involving invariant dynamically faithful states or internal classical reference frames. For locally tomographic parent theories, we prove that every theory symmetry admits a representation by linear system actions and that the invariant subtheory satisfies process tomography. An invariant multipartite process space fails local tomography if and only if some bipartition has sides sharing a non-trivial irreducible representation. We characterise when ancillary systems are necessary, which representations they must carry, and when entanglement is required for ancilla-free process tomography. We develop a framework for unifying twirled subtheories and extend incoherent simulations to compact groups. Finally, we recover bilocal classical theory as a twirled subtheory of classical theory and real quantum theory as a swirled subtheory of complex quantum theory, deriving their tomographic properties from their representation structure.

pending.title: Learning Midcircuit Measurement Backaction from Three Repeated Measurements
authors: Chia-Tung Chu, Su-un Lee, Han Zheng, Senrui Chen, Bibek Pokharel, Alireza Seif, and Liang Jiang
pending.abstract: Accurate modeling of midcircuit measurements (MCMs) is essential for dynamic-circuit operations such as syndrome extraction, measurement-based reset, and the separation of state-preparation and measurement error. Unlike terminal measurement, a noisy MCM both produces a classical outcome and alters t…

pending.title: Spreading of Magic Resource under Unitary Clifford Dynamics
authors: Mircea Bejan, Pieter W. Claeys, and Jiangtian Yao
pending.abstract: Nonstabilizerness, or quantum magic resource, presents a valuable resource in quantum error correction and computation. We study the dynamics of locally injected nonstabilizerness in unitary Clifford circuits, where the total nonstabilizerness is conserved. However, the absence of physical observables quantifying nonstabilizerness precludes a direct microscopic or hydrodynamic description of its local distribution and dynamics. Using insights from stabilizer quantum error correcting codes, we rigorously show that the spatial distribution of nonstabilizerness can be inferred from a canonical representation of low-magic states, dubbed the bipartite magic gauge. Moreover, we propose two operationally relevant magic length scales. We numerically establish that, at early times, both length scales grow ballistically at distinct velocities set by the entanglement velocity, after which nonstabilizerness delocalizes. Our Letter sheds light on the spatiotemporal structure of quantum resources and complexity in many-body dynamics, opening up avenues for investigating their transport properties and further connections with quantum error correction.

pending.title: Optimal quantum discrimination at Liouvillian exceptional points
pending.abstract: Central to non-Hermitian sensing is the question of whether exceptional points (EPs) can make weak perturbations easier to detect. We show that despite enhanced spectral response, in finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap, EPs offer no fundamental advantage in how the observation time required for reliable detection of a weak perturbation scales with the perturbation strength. We nevertheless demonstrate that by selectively choosing perturbations that enhance the quantum Fisher information rate, EPs can shorten the observation time needed to reach a predefined detection accuracy relative to a comparable non-EP reference at the same decay rate. As an illustration, we show using an optomechanical model at an EP that we can detect a weak force through the cavity output at the same reliability in less time than a non-EP reference. Our results establish fundamental limits on perturbation detection at EPs and can guide the design of faster non-Hermitian sensors based on optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and trapped ions.

pending.title: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes
pending.abstract: We construct a rank-one minimal informationally complete measurement (MIC) with an invertible dual operator and prove that, for arbitrary finite input and output dimensions, a channel universally preserves measurement incompatibility if and only if its input space contains a noiseless code subspace of the full output dimension. Preserving the compatibility threshold of a finite family of binary measurements already guarantees such a code. Furthermore, for every $d\ge2$, there exists a family of binary measurements that is incompatible on the full space but compatible after compression to any proper subspace. These results resolve the conjecture of Chitambar and Zhang and the existence question posed by Uola and coauthors. We also give an explicit construction of exact encodings and show that, for a sufficiently small shift in the compatibility threshold, the transmission error of an approximate encoding is bounded by a constant times the square of the shift. These results establish a connection between measurement compatibility, quantum steering, and quantum error correction.

pending.title: Matrix Samplers and Quantum-Proof Extractors: Their Correspondence and Almost-Optimal Constructions
pending.abstract: We establish an equivalence between matrix samplers and quantum-proof randomness extractors. The classical sampler--extractor equivalence is established by a seminal work of Zuckerman (Random Structures & Algorithms, 1997). Using this equivalence, we construct explicit strong matrix samplers with optimal randomness overhead and near-optimal sample complexity via constructing quantum-proof extractors. Specifically for matrix dimension $D$, accuracy $\varepsilon$ and failure probability $δ\leq\varepsilon$, our matrix sampler uses $m+O_α(\log(D/δ))$ random bits and $O_α(\varepsilon^{-2-α}\log^{1+α}(D/δ))$ samples, for any constant $α>0$. Compared with the matrix sampler of Xun and Zuckerman (CCC 2025), our construction has improvements in two aspects. Under the same optimal random seed length, we can replace the $\operatorname{poly} D$ dependence in the number of samples by $O(\log^{1-γ} D)$. Under the same scale of sample size, we can remove their $\log\log D$ factor in the length of the random seed. Our underlying strong quantum-proof extractor has output length $n-O_α(a+\log(1/η))$ and seed length at most $(1+α)\log a+(2+α)\log(1/η)+O_α(1)$ for $n$-bit sources with conditional min-entropy $n-a$ and error $η$. We also obtain strong quantum-proof extractors for every constant entropy rate, for any error as small as $2^{-Ω(n)}$, having optimal seed length $O(\log(n/η))$ and output length $Ω(n)$, improving previous constructions.

pending.title: Generative quantum extreme learning machines
pending.abstract: Training the circuit of a quantum generative model is hampered by barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with the number of qubits. In the present work we propose a generative protocol based on the paradigm of quantum extreme learning machines, in which the circuit is never trained. A random latent vector is encoded into a quantum state, evolved with a fixed unitary and measured, and only a linear output layer is trained. The encoding of the latent variable determines the functions available to the model, while the unitary decides which combinations of them are seen by the trained layer. With the help of Pauli propagation we show that for a Clifford unitary each feature is a single product of sines and cosines of the encoded angles, so that a Clifford circuit, even a strongly entangling one, does not create new functions. Doping the circuit with $T$ gates mixes these products and changes the nonstabilizerness of the state, but the space of functions remains the one fixed by the encoding. For brickworks of Haar-random two-qubit gates the features are no longer single products, and their variation with the latent variable decreases with the depth of the circuit. For the proposed encoding and for one- and two-dimensional distributions, generated both from expectation values and from single measurements, neither the entanglement produced by a Clifford reservoir nor the additional nonstabilizerness of Haar-random brickworks systematically improves the generator, and a reservoir with no gates at all is competitive with entangling circuits.

pending.title: Ancestor Lifting of Quasi-Cyclic Additive Codes and Certified Quantum Codes
pending.abstract: Additive codes over $\Ffour$ that are self-orthogonal under the trace inner product correspond to binary quantum stabilizer codes. We study 1-generator $(1,2)$-quasi-cyclic (QC) additive codes and their exact quantum distances. For composite lengths $n=\ell m$, an ancestor-lifting theorem transports dual words of the folded ancestor to the length-$n$ code. A two-layer decomposition for $\ell=2$ and a CRT splitting for odd $\ell$ yield dimension laws and explain equality, escape, and mixed-branch behavior in the certified examples. A palindromic criterion ensures symplectic self-orthogonality, while reversal pairing and a symplectic Gram rank formula describe broader construction families. Exact distances are established by information-set decoding screening, Brouwer--Zimmermann computation on the additive dual, and independent witness verification. We certify twenty-one record-breaking binary quantum codes across twenty entries of Grassl's code table, with twenty-eight certified members in total. Propagation improves thirty-four further entries, and explicit constructions are supplied for three table-tying GV entries marked Code Missing Construction. Six additional candidates are reported only with rigorous upper bounds and heuristic screening evidence. The results connect divisor-lattice structure in additive quasi-cyclic codes with reproducible certification of exact quantum distances.

pending.title: Quantum State Preparation for Complex-Valued Amplitudes
pending.abstract: We present a state preparation procedure that takes binary registers containing the real and imaginary parts of a complex number $z=x+iy$ and prepares an amplitude approximating $z/α$, where $α$ is a normalization constant. The magnitude and argument are computed using the Coordinate Rotation Digital Computer (CORDIC) algorithm. We then encode the magnitude into an amplitude, and apply phase gates to introduce the argument. A reversible in-place multiplier allows the coordinate updates to use fixed precision while clearing their temporary workspace. The procedure uses $O(n^2)$ $T$ gates and $O(n)$ additional qubits. Compared with separately encoding the real and imaginary parts and combining them through LCU, the construction can allow a smaller normalization and reduce amplitude-amplification costs. The computed polar representation also remains available for further arithmetic before amplitude-encoding.

pending.title: Experimental Geometric State Preparation on the Bloch Sphere Via Linear Mechanical Resonator
pending.abstract: The Bloch sphere representation, familiar from quantum two-level systems, can also describe classical linear systems whose dynamics are effectively confined to two modes. Here, we experimentally realize this framework in a linear two-mass, three-spring mechanical system by controlling superpositions of its symmetric and antisymmetric eigenmodes. The system is driven from both boundaries at a fixed frequency between the two resonances, so that the steady-state response remains within a two-mode manifold. By independently varying the relative amplitude and phase of the boundary excitations, we generate tunable modal superpositions. Scanning laser vibrometer measurements and frequency-domain analysis are used to extract the complex modal coefficients, which are then normalized and mapped onto Bloch sphere coordinates. This reconstruction reveals planar rotations of the state under phase sweeps and continuous steering between eigenstates under amplitude-ratio tuning. These results provide an experimental validation of Bloch sphere state reconstruction and steady-state geometric state preparation in a minimal linear mass-spring platform, establishing a simple classical testbed for exploring two-mode manifold dynamics.

pending.title: An algebraic characterisation of $n$-qubit pure-state invariants
pending.abstract: We study the set of $n$-qubit pure quantum states. Specifically, we consider their incarnation as density matrices in Bloch representation. Building on prior work, we define a family of quadratic functions in Pauli expectation values, and fully characterise all instances that result in state-independent purity constraints. The resulting family of pure-state invariants is surprisingly rich in structure, with strong ties to the geometry of symplectic polar spaces. After charting the general landscape, we define a sub-family of pure-state invariants that satisfies the dynamical constraint of being stable under state update. We prove that it corresponds with (different embeddings of) symplectic Lie algebras $\mathfrak{sp}(2^{n-1})\subset\mathfrak{su}(2^n)$, which admit a generating set of Pauli operators. We carefully distinguish the symplectic case from its orthogonal counterpart, using the Arf invariant of quadratic refinements of the symplectic form on the projective Pauli group, which we further identify with quaternionic structures on $\mathbb{C}^{2^n}$ that are both generated by and restricted to Pauli operators. As a consequence of this analysis, we reveal previously largely overlooked structure in the $n$-qubit Pauli group. We highlight this in a number of examples. We characterise all state-independent uncertainty relations in variance for Pauli observables, as well as all Pauli channels for which the output fidelity and output purity are state-independent. We further show that the orbits of the projective stabiliser groups of pure-state invariants, which for $n\geq2$ are proper subgroups of the Clifford group, form complex projective state $2$-designs, while their unitary lifts form symplectic $2$-designs.

pending.title: Equilibrium Learning of Quantum Circuits
pending.abstract: Equilibrium learning trains a physical system using observables of its relaxed states. We extend this principle to gate-based quantum circuits by embedding a parametrized circuit in a Feynman-Kitaev (FK) Hamiltonian and imposing the compilation target either through an output clamping term or through a target-dependent cyclic condition on the clock register. The ground state energies and the overlaps of the corresponding ground states with the free history state define faithful cost functions for unitary and state compilation. We show that these costs are nonlinear functions of the compilation infidelity and therefore reshape the optimization landscape. We show that starting from the free history state, quantum phase estimation can prepare the relevant ground states and estimate the cost functions with polynomial resources. In two-qubit benchmarks, optimization with the equilibrium cost functions reaches a fixed fidelity threshold in fewer sweeps than standard compilation infidelity cost function for many instances. The results demonstrate the potential for encoding quantum learning problems as computation of equilibrium observables.

pending.title: AlgebrasTQD: Computing Algebras and Interfaces in Twisted Quantum Doubles
pending.abstract: We present AlgebrasTQD, an open-source code written in GAP (Groups, Algorithms, and Programming), for computing condensable algebras and the corresponding topological boundaries and interfaces of twisted quantum doubles $D^ω(G)$. These algebras can be used to classify 1+1d gapped and gapless phases whose symmetry is related by gauging to a finite group $G$ with anomaly $ω\in H^3(G,U(1))$, to study 2+1d anyon proliferation and to construct logical gates in non-Abelian topological quantum codes. The functions in AlgebrasTQD compute all condensable algebras $A(H,F,γ,ε)$ with their algebra structure and anyons, sort them into isomorphism classes and identify the twin algebras that are inequivalent but share the same anyon decomposition. AlgebrasTQD also determines all the subalgebra relations, the corresponding Hasse diagram and the types of 1+1d phases for any chosen, possibly non-invertible, group-theoretical symmetry. For non-maximal algebras, the code computes the reduced topological order with its $3$-cocycle and the map of anyons across the topological interface. Finally, AlgebrasTQD includes functions that construct certain non-Clifford logical gates via non-Abelian surface codes. We summarize the formulas that are implemented in the AlgebrasTQD code, and we illustrate its use with Abelian and non-Abelian groups including $\mathbb{Z}_2^3$ with $ω_\text{III}$, $D_8$, $A_4$ with and without anomaly, twin algebras and twin phases, and the Clifford-hierarchy gates in quantum doubles of dihedral groups. All arithmetic is exact and AlgebrasTQD can be used with any finite group $G$ and 3-cocycle $ω$, limited only by the time and size of the calculation. The code is available at https://github.com/AlisonWarman/AlgebrasTQD

pending.title: Certifying Localizable Quantum Properties with Constant Sample Complexity
authors: Zhenyu Du, Jinchang Liu, Elias X. Huber, Zi-Wen Liu, and Xiongfeng Ma
pending.abstract: Characterizing increasingly complex quantum systems is a central task in quantum information science, yet experimental costs often scale prohibitively with system size. Certifying key properties using simple local measurements is highly desirable but challenging. In this work, we introduce a highly general certification framework based on a physical phenomenon that we call localizable quantumness: for generic many-body states, essential quantum properties are robustly preserved within the projected ensembles on small subsystems after performing local projective measurements on the rest of the system. Leveraging this insight, we develop protocols to certify global properties—including multipartite entanglement, circuit complexity, and quantum magic—by witnessing them on a small, accessible subsystem. Remarkably, randomizing the local measurement bases extends this capability to certify state fidelity. Relying solely on local Pauli measurements, these protocols achieve constant sample complexity and robustness for almost all quantum states, including a wide range of physically relevant states. For certifying the fidelity of n -qubit states, this O ( 1 ) scaling dramatically improves upon state-of-the-art protocols requiring O ( n 4 ) samples. Our unified framework provides both a practical toolkit for large-scale quantum certification and a novel lens into complex many-body systems.

pending.title: Bidirectional Teleportation Using Scrambling Dynamics: A Practical Protocol
authors: Amit Vikram, Edwin Chaparro, Muhammad Miskeen Khan, Andrew Lucas, Chris Akers, and Ana Maria Rey
pending.abstract: We show that quantum information scrambling can enable a generic swap gate between collective degrees of freedom in systems without universal local control.
